questions.stem: A structural biologist solves the crystal structure of a human MHC class I molecule and focuses on the cleft that binds an 8- to 11-amino-acid peptide. The alpha1 and alpha2 domains that form this peptide-binding groove are contributed by which of the following?

choices.label: D
choices.text: The alpha chain and a beta chain

explanation.summary: The MHC class I peptide-binding groove is formed by the alpha1 and alpha2 domains, both located on the single alpha chain.
explanation.whyCorrect: An MHC class I molecule is composed of an alpha chain (with alpha1, alpha2, and alpha3 domains) noncovalently associated with beta-2-microglobulin. The brick states that the alpha1 and alpha2 domains form a cleft that binds and holds peptides for T cell recognition, and both of these domains belong to the alpha chain. Therefore the groove is built from the alpha chain alone.

whyWrongByChoice.A: MHC class I contains no beta chain; its second subunit is beta-2-microglobulin.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Beta-2-microglobulin has no role in forming the peptide-binding cleft of class I.
whyWrongByChoice.D: It is MHC class II, not class I, whose groove is formed by an alpha and a beta chain (alpha1 plus beta1).
whyWrongByChoice.E: Beta-2-microglobulin associates with the alpha chain and stabilizes class I, but it does not contribute to the peptide-binding groove.

questions.stem: A mutant antigen-presenting cell line assembles MHC class II normally and transports it to the surface, but the class II molecules still carry CLIP in their groove and fail to display extracellular peptides to CD4 T cells. Deficiency of which protein best explains this defect?

explanation.summary: HLA-DM catalyzes the exchange of CLIP for an antigenic peptide in the endosome; without it, MHC class II remains stuck with CLIP.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explains that after the invariant chain is degraded in acidic endosomes, a fragment called CLIP remains in the MHC II groove. The chaperone HLA-DM then catalyzes the exchange of CLIP for an antigenic peptide. If HLA-DM is missing, CLIP cannot be swapped out, so class II reaches the surface still occupied by CLIP and cannot present real peptides.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Beta-2-microglobulin is a subunit of MHC class I and plays no part in class II peptide loading.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Loss of the invariant chain would leave the groove open (no CLIP), not stuck with CLIP; the invariant chain is the source of CLIP, not its remover.
whyWrongByChoice.D: TAP transports peptides from the cytosol into the ER for class I loading; it is not involved in the class II CLIP exchange.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tapasin functions in MHC class I loading, tethering class I to TAP, and has no role in CLIP removal from class II.

questions.stem: A fibroblast is infected with cytomegalovirus, which produces a protein that prevents peptides from being transported from the cytosol into the endoplasmic reticulum. As a result, the cell can no longer display peptides on MHC class I. The viral protein directly inhibits which of the following?

explanation.summary: TAP (transporter associated with antigen processing) moves proteasome-derived peptides from the cytosol into the ER for MHC class I loading.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes that peptide fragments generated by the proteasome are transported into the ER by TAP, which prefers peptides 8 to 16 amino acids long. Blocking peptide transport from cytosol into the ER is exactly TAP's function, and the case connection notes that cytomegalovirus can block TAP so that MHC class I cannot be loaded and is not expressed.

whyWrongByChoice.A: HLA-DM works in the MHC class II endosomal pathway, not in transporting peptides into the ER.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Tapasin tethers MHC class I near TAP but does not itself transport peptides across the ER membrane; the described step is transport, which is TAP.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The invariant chain functions in class II loading and has nothing to do with peptide transport into the ER.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The proteasome still generates peptides in the cytosol; the block described is at the transport step, downstream of the proteasome.

questions.stem: A virus blocks TAP in an infected cell so that little or no MHC class I reaches the surface, preventing CD8 cytotoxic T cells from recognizing the infection. Which cell of the immune system is nonetheless able to eliminate this MHC class I-deficient cell?

explanation.summary: Natural killer cells are inhibited by MHC class I on healthy cells and kill cells that have lost it, overcoming viral TAP blockade.
explanation.whyCorrect: The case connection explains that MHC class I inhibits natural killer cells, so the absence of MHC class I on a cell reduces this inhibition. This allows natural killer cells to kill the infected cell and overcome the virus's ability to block TAP and hide from CD8 T cells.

whyWrongByChoice.A: CD8 cytotoxic T cells require peptide displayed on MHC class I, which is exactly what is missing here, so they cannot act.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Eosinophils primarily target parasites and are not the effector that kills MHC class I-low cells.
whyWrongByChoice.C: CD4 helper T cells recognize peptide on MHC class II and do not directly kill MHC class I-deficient cells.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Plasma cells secrete antibody; they do not kill virus-infected cells by recognizing loss of MHC class I.

questions.stem: A virus-infected nucleated cell displays a viral peptide on MHC class I. A T cell binds this complex through its T cell receptor and its CD8 co-receptor, becomes activated, and then triggers the infected cell to undergo apoptosis. Which mechanism does this T cell use to kill the target?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Phagocytosing and digesting the infected cell

choices.label: B
choices.text: Presenting the viral antigen on its own MHC class II

choices.label: C
choices.text: Producing cytokines that help B cells make antibody

choices.label: D
choices.text: Releasing perforin and granzymes to induce apoptosis

choices.label: E
choices.text: Secreting antibody that opsonizes the infected cell

explanation.summary: Activated CD8 cytotoxic T cells release perforin and granzymes to induce apoptosis in the target cell.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that once activated, CD8 cytotoxic T cells release perforin and granzymes, inducing apoptosis in the target cell. CD8 binds MHC class I and stabilizes the interaction between the TCR and MHC, allowing the cytotoxic T cell to recognize and kill virus-infected cells.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cytotoxic T cells kill via cytotoxic granules; phagocytosis is performed by macrophages and other phagocytes.
whyWrongByChoice.B: CD8 T cells recognize peptide on MHC class I; they are effectors that kill, not antigen-presenting cells that display on MHC class II.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Secreting cytokines to help B cells is a function of CD4 helper T cells, not CD8 cytotoxic T cells.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Antibody is produced by B cells and plasma cells, not by cytotoxic T cells.

questions.stem: A dendritic cell displays a bacterial peptide on MHC class II. A T cell binds this complex using its T cell receptor and its CD4 co-receptor. Once activated, this T cell releases cytokines that drive B cells to make antibody and help activate macrophages. Which cell is being described?

explanation.summary: CD4 helper T cells recognize peptide on MHC class II and, once activated, secrete cytokines that promote antibody production and activate other immune cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that helper T cells express CD4, a co-receptor that binds MHC class II and stabilizes the TCR-MHC interaction. Once activated, CD4 helper T cells stimulate other lymphocytes through cytokines and stimulatory molecules, promoting antibody production by B cells and the activation of macrophages, cytotoxic T cells, and other immune cells.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The B cell is the recipient of helper T cell signals here, not the CD4-expressing helper being described.
whyWrongByChoice.C: CD8 cytotoxic T cells read peptide on MHC class I and kill target cells; they do not use the CD4 co-receptor.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Natural killer cells are innate lymphocytes with no T cell receptor or CD4 co-receptor.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Neutrophils are phagocytes of the innate system and are not T cells.

questions.stem: A 26-year-old traveler develops malaria, and Plasmodium parasites persist inside mature erythrocytes despite an otherwise intact CD8 T cell response. Which feature of mature erythrocytes best explains why CD8 cytotoxic T cells fail to detect the intracellular parasite?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Erythrocytes are destroyed too quickly by natural killer cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: Erythrocytes express high levels of HLA-DM

choices.label: C
choices.text: Erythrocytes express only MHC class II

choices.label: D
choices.text: Erythrocytes lack a nucleus and do not express MHC class I

choices.label: E
choices.text: Erythrocytes secrete antibody that shields the parasite

explanation.summary: Because mature erythrocytes have no nucleus, they do not express MHC class I, so intracellular parasites escape CD8 T cell detection.
explanation.whyCorrect: The clinical correlation states that every nucleated cell expresses MHC class I, but erythrocytes lack a nucleus and therefore do not express MHC class I. As a result, CD8 T cells cannot detect a virus or intracellular parasite inside red cells, which is how the malaria parasite escapes detection and persists.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The escape is due to lack of MHC class I, not rapid killing by natural killer cells.
whyWrongByChoice.B: HLA-DM is a class II loading chaperone found in antigen-presenting cells, not in erythrocytes, and is irrelevant here.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Erythrocytes do not express MHC class II either; the point is the absence of MHC class I.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Erythrocytes do not produce antibody; only B cells and plasma cells do.

questions.stem: Because MHC genes are expressed codominantly, a nucleated cell displays MHC class I molecules encoded by both the maternal and paternal copies of the HLA-A, HLA-B, and HLA-C loci. In a person heterozygous at all three loci, how many different MHC class I molecules are expressed on the cell surface?

explanation.summary: Three class I loci (HLA-A, -B, -C), each expressed codominantly from two inherited haplotypes, yield six different MHC class I molecules.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explains that MHC genes are codominant and that you inherit two haplotypes, giving two copies of each gene. With three class I loci (HLA-A, HLA-B, HLA-C) and two alleles each, a heterozygous person expresses 6 different MHC class I molecules on the cell surface.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Expressing only one molecule would ignore the three separate loci and codominant expression of both alleles.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Two would reflect a single locus with two alleles, not all three class I loci.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Three would count each locus only once and ignore that both parental alleles are expressed.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Twelve double-counts; there are three class I loci times two alleles, which equals six, not twelve.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old woman has chronic diarrhea, weight loss, and duodenal biopsy showing villous atrophy consistent with celiac disease. More than 90% of patients with this condition carry a particular set of class II alleles. Which HLA gene is most strongly associated with celiac disease?

explanation.summary: Celiac disease is strongly linked to specific class II HLA-DQ alleles (HLA-DQA1*05 and HLA-DQB1*02).
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick notes that some MHC alleles are associated with autoimmune diseases and gives the example that more than 90% of people with celiac disease carry HLA-DQA1*05 (group 5 of the DQ alpha chains) and HLA-DQB1*02. HLA-DQ is a class II gene encoding both alpha and beta chains.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Beta-2-microglobulin is an invariant class I subunit, not a polymorphic disease-associated class II allele.
whyWrongByChoice.B: HLA-A is a class I locus encoding an alpha chain and is not the celiac association described.
whyWrongByChoice.C: HLA-B is a class I locus and is not the gene linked to celiac disease here.
whyWrongByChoice.D: HLA-C is also a class I locus, not the class II gene associated with celiac disease.

questions.stem: A patient receives a kidney transplant. The transplant team notes that the more closely the donor and recipient HLA genes are matched, the slower and milder any rejection tends to be. Which statement best explains why a mismatched graft is rejected?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Beta-2-microglobulin is completely absent from donor cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: Donor cells lack all HLA genes and cannot be recognized

choices.label: C
choices.text: Rejection speed is independent of how well the MHC is matched

choices.label: D
choices.text: The recipient recognizes the donor MHC molecules as self

choices.label: E
choices.text: The recipient's T cells recognize the donor MHC molecules as foreign

explanation.summary: Transplant rejection occurs because the recipient's immune system sees the donor's different MHC molecules as foreign.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explains that people recognize their own MHC molecules as self and do not react to them, but a transplant with different MHC molecules is seen as foreign, prompting the immune system to attack. It also states that the speed and severity of rejection depend on how closely the donor and recipient are matched, which is why careful HLA sequencing helps.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Beta-2-microglobulin is present on donor cells; its absence is not the cause of rejection.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Donor cells do express HLA molecules; the problem is that they differ from the recipient's, not that they are absent.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The brick specifically states that rejection speed and severity depend on how closely the MHC is matched.
whyWrongByChoice.D: If donor MHC were recognized as self, there would be no rejection; rejection happens precisely because it is seen as foreign.

questions.stem: A dendritic cell engulfs a virally infected apoptotic cell and its debris. Although these viral proteins originated outside the dendritic cell, the dendritic cell displays viral peptides on MHC class I to activate CD8 T cells while also presenting on MHC class II to CD4 T cells. This process is best described as which of the following?

explanation.summary: Cross-presentation is the loading of exogenous (externally derived) antigens onto MHC class I, allowing activation of both CD4 and CD8 T cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explains that during an infection both CD4 and CD8 T cells must be activated. Peptides taken up in a phagosome can leak out and be loaded into MHC class I as though they were endogenous, even though they came from outside the cell. This is called cross-presentation, and it lets dendritic cells present viral peptides to both CD4 and CD8 T cells.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Central tolerance is the removal of self-reactive lymphocytes during development, not antigen presentation across MHC classes.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Clonal deletion is the elimination of self-reactive clones, not the described presentation pathway.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Opsonization is the coating of a pathogen by antibody or complement to enhance phagocytosis, not antigen presentation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Positive selection is a thymic step in T cell development, unrelated to presenting exogenous antigen on MHC class I.

questions.stem: In a professional antigen-presenting cell, newly synthesized MHC class II must be prevented from binding peptides in the endoplasmic reticulum before it reaches the endosome. Which protein occupies the MHC class II groove in the ER to block premature peptide loading?

explanation.summary: The invariant chain, through its CLIP segment, sits in the MHC class II groove in the ER and blocks premature peptide binding.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that professional APCs make MHC class II in the ER, where the chaperone invariant chain binds it. A part of the invariant chain called the class II invariant chain peptide (CLIP) rests in the MHC class II peptide-binding groove and blocks other peptides from binding until the molecule reaches the endosome.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Beta-2-microglobulin is a structural subunit of MHC class I and is not involved in class II groove protection.
whyWrongByChoice.B: HLA-DM acts later, in the acidic endosome, to remove CLIP; it does not occupy the groove in the ER to block loading.
whyWrongByChoice.D: TAP transports peptides into the ER for class I loading and does not block the class II groove.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tapasin functions in MHC class I loading by bridging class I to TAP; it does not occupy the class II groove.

questions.stem: A researcher isolates a clone of T cells and a clone of B cells, both specific for the same viral envelope protein. When the intact, soluble envelope protein is added to culture, the B cells bind it through their antigen receptors, but the T cells do not respond until antigen-presenting cells are added. Which property of the T cell antigen receptor best explains this difference?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It binds only antigens longer than 30 amino acids

choices.label: B
choices.text: It binds only carbohydrate antigens on pathogen surfaces

choices.label: C
choices.text: It recognizes intact antigen only after secretion as antibody

choices.label: D
choices.text: It recognizes only peptide antigen loaded into MHC

choices.label: E
choices.text: It requires prior opsonization of the antigen by complement

explanation.summary: T cell receptors are MHC-restricted, whereas B cell receptors can bind whole, intact antigen.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that B cell antigen receptors (BCRs) can recognize and bind whole, intact antigens, while T cell antigen receptors (TCRs) are MHC-restricted, meaning they can only recognize peptide antigen loaded into MHC. This is why the T cell clone needs antigen-presenting cells to process the protein into peptides and display them on MHC before it can respond.

whyWrongByChoice.A: MHC-restricted recognition involves short peptides (8 to 11 or 10 to 30 amino acids), not large intact antigens.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The TCR recognizes peptide in MHC, not carbohydrate; the restriction is to peptide-MHC, not to a sugar antigen.
whyWrongByChoice.C: T cells do not secrete antibody; the TCR remains a surface receptor that reads peptide-MHC complexes.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Opsonization enhances phagocytosis and is not a requirement for TCR recognition of antigen.

questions.stem: An HLA-DR molecule from a patient binds a set of peptides different from those bound by the same HLA-DR molecule in most people. Sequencing reveals a single amino acid substitution in the beta chain. This substitution is most likely located in which domain?

explanation.summary: The peptide-binding cleft of MHC class II is formed by portions of the alpha1 and beta1 domains, so a beta-chain change that alters peptide binding lies in beta1.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explains that an MHC II molecule is composed of noncovalently associated alpha and beta chains, each with two main domains, and that portions of the alpha1 and beta1 domains form the peptide-binding cleft. Population variation in the amino acids that make up this groove alters which peptides can bind. A beta-chain substitution that changes peptide specificity must therefore lie in the beta1 domain.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Alpha2 in MHC class II is the membrane-proximal domain of the alpha chain, not part of the cleft, and it is on the alpha chain rather than the beta chain.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Beta-2-microglobulin is a subunit of MHC class I, not a domain of the MHC class II beta chain.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Beta2 is the membrane-proximal domain of the beta chain and does not form the peptide-binding cleft.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Alpha3 is a domain of the MHC class I alpha chain; MHC class II has no alpha3 domain.

questions.stem: An investigator compares how MHC class I and MHC class II molecules are anchored in the plasma membrane. Which of the following correctly describes the number of transmembrane regions contributed by the chains of each molecule?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Class I has one; class II has one

choices.label: B
choices.text: Class I has one; class II has two

choices.label: C
choices.text: Class I has three; class II has two

choices.label: D
choices.text: Class I has two; class II has one

choices.label: E
choices.text: Class I has two; class II has two

explanation.summary: MHC class I is anchored only by the transmembrane region of its alpha chain, whereas both the alpha and beta chains of MHC class II have transmembrane domains.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes the MHC I alpha chain as having alpha1, alpha2, and alpha3 domains as well as a transmembrane region, with beta-2-microglobulin noncovalently associated and lacking a membrane anchor. For MHC II, both the alpha and beta chains have two main domains and transmembrane domains. Thus class I has a single transmembrane region and class II has two.

whyWrongByChoice.A: MHC class II has two chains that each span the membrane, so it does not have only one transmembrane region.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The three domains of the class I alpha chain (alpha1, alpha2, alpha3) are extracellular; only one transmembrane region exists.
whyWrongByChoice.D: This reverses the pattern; it is class II, with its alpha and beta chains, that has two transmembrane regions.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Beta-2-microglobulin does not span the membrane, so MHC class I has only one transmembrane region, not two.

questions.stem: A 25-amino-acid peptide derived from a bacterial protein is tested in a binding assay against purified MHC molecules. Based on the peptide lengths each class of MHC accommodates, this peptide is expected to bind which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Both MHC class I and MHC class II

choices.label: D
choices.text: Neither class until it is tagged with ubiquitin

choices.label: E
choices.text: Neither class until it is trimmed to 8 amino acids

explanation.summary: MHC class II loads peptides 10 to 30 amino acids long, whereas MHC class I holds only 8- to 11-amino-acid peptides.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that MHC I molecules hold peptides that are 8 to 11 amino acids long, while MHC II can load peptides 10 to 30 amino acids in length (APCs typically load peptides of 15 to 25 amino acids). A 25-amino-acid peptide is far too long for the class I groove but falls within the range accommodated by class II.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Only class II can accommodate this length; class I cannot bind a peptide of 25 amino acids.
whyWrongByChoice.B: A 25-amino-acid peptide exceeds the 8- to 11-amino-acid limit of the MHC class I groove.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Ubiquitin tags cytosolic proteins for proteasomal degradation; it is not a prerequisite for a peptide to bind MHC.
whyWrongByChoice.E: No trimming is required for class II binding; 25 amino acids is within the 10 to 30 range for MHC II.

questions.stem: A cytosolic viral protein is degraded by the proteasome, and one of the resulting 14-amino-acid fragments is transported into the endoplasmic reticulum. Despite entering the ER, this fragment is not displayed on the cell surface by MHC class I. Which of the following best explains this finding?

choices.label: A
choices.text: MHC class I holds only peptides 8 to 11 amino acids long

choices.label: B
choices.text: TAP cannot transport peptides longer than 11 amino acids

choices.label: C
choices.text: Tapasin blocks peptides longer than 11 amino acids from entering the ER

choices.label: D
choices.text: The fragment must first be exchanged for CLIP by HLA-DM

choices.label: E
choices.text: The fragment was never tagged with ubiquitin

explanation.summary: TAP transports peptides of 8 to 16 amino acids, but MHC class I can load only those 8 to 11 amino acids long, so a 14-mer enters the ER yet cannot be presented.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick notes that the proteasome generates diverse sizes of peptide fragments and that TAP preferentially chooses peptides 8 to 16 amino acids in length for transport into the ER. However, MHC I can only load peptides that are 8 to 11 amino acids long. A 14-amino-acid fragment is within TAP's range, explaining its arrival in the ER, but it is too long for the class I groove, so it is not presented.

whyWrongByChoice.B: TAP preferentially transports peptides of 8 to 16 amino acids, so a 14-mer is within its range, consistent with the fragment reaching the ER.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Tapasin brings MHC I close to TAP to facilitate loading; it does not act as a size filter at the ER membrane.
whyWrongByChoice.D: CLIP and HLA-DM belong to the MHC class II loading pathway in endosomes, not to class I loading in the ER.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Ubiquitination targets the intact protein to the proteasome; the protein was already degraded, so ubiquitin tagging is not the missing step.

questions.stem: A transplant center performs high-resolution sequencing of a recipient's HLA-A, HLA-B, HLA-C, HLA-DP, HLA-DQ, and HLA-DR genes to identify a well-matched donor. These genes are clustered together on which chromosome?

explanation.summary: The human MHC genes, called HLA genes, are located together on chromosome 6.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that the genes that code for MHC are located on chromosome 6 and that human MHC genes are called human leukocyte antigen (HLA) genes. The class I locus (HLA-A, -B, -C) and class II locus (HLA-DP, -DQ, -DR) sit close together on this chromosome, which is why they are often inherited together as a haplotype.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Chromosome 2 does not carry the HLA region.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Chromosome 14 does not carry the HLA region.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Chromosome 15 encodes beta-2-microglobulin, which is not part of the MHC locus.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Chromosome 22 does not carry the HLA region.

questions.stem: A laboratory sequences the entire HLA region of chromosome 6 in a patient awaiting transplantation. Which of the following components of MHC class I molecules is encoded by a gene located outside this region, on chromosome 15?

explanation.summary: Beta-2-microglobulin is encoded on chromosome 15 and is not part of the MHC class I loci on chromosome 6.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that for MHC I, the HLA-A, HLA-B, and HLA-C genes encode the alpha chains, while beta-2-microglobulin is encoded on chromosome 15 and is not encoded in the MHC I loci. Sequencing only the HLA region on chromosome 6 would therefore not capture the gene for this class I subunit.

whyWrongByChoice.B: HLA-A lies within the class I MHC locus on chromosome 6.
whyWrongByChoice.C: HLA-B lies within the class I MHC locus on chromosome 6.
whyWrongByChoice.D: HLA-C lies within the class I MHC locus on chromosome 6.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The HLA-DR beta chain is a class II component and is encoded within the class II locus on chromosome 6, not on chromosome 15.

questions.stem: A patient's MHC class II molecules are found to carry a variant beta chain that alters peptide presentation by HLA-DR. Which of the following genes encodes this chain?

explanation.summary: MHC class II gene names include a designation for the alpha and beta chains, so the HLA-DR beta chain is encoded by HLA-DRB.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explains that the HLA-DP, HLA-DQ, and HLA-DR genes encode both the alpha and beta chains of MHC II, and that the MHC II gene names include a designation of alpha and beta chains, for example HLA-DRA and HLA-DRB. A variant HLA-DR beta chain therefore arises from HLA-DRB.

whyWrongByChoice.A: HLA-A encodes the alpha chain of an MHC class I molecule, not a class II beta chain.
whyWrongByChoice.B: HLA-B encodes the alpha chain of an MHC class I molecule.
whyWrongByChoice.C: HLA-C encodes the alpha chain of an MHC class I molecule.
whyWrongByChoice.D: HLA-DRA encodes the alpha chain of HLA-DR, not the beta chain.

questions.stem: HLA typing is performed on a patient and several potential organ donors. According to the standard convention for naming HLA alleles, which of the following pairs of alleles belong to the same major group?

explanation.summary: The number immediately after the asterisk identifies the major allele group; numbers after the colon indicate differences within that group.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explains that the major group of an HLA allele is indicated by a separator (asterisk) and a number, followed by colons and additional numbers conveying differences within the major group. It gives the example that HLA-A*01 and HLA-A*02 are two major groups, and that HLA-A*01:01 and HLA-A*01:37 differ by sequence but are both in the same major group.

whyWrongByChoice.B: HLA-A*01 and HLA-A*02 are two different major groups of HLA-A alleles.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The major group is determined by the number before the colon (01 versus 02), so these are different major groups despite the shared 37.
whyWrongByChoice.D: HLA-B and HLA-C are different class I genes, so their alleles cannot belong to the same major group.
whyWrongByChoice.E: These are alleles of two different genes (HLA-A and HLA-B); sharing the number 02 does not place them in the same group.

questions.stem: A macrophage is obtained from a person who is heterozygous at every HLA locus. Counting both class I and class II, how many different MHC molecules are expected on the surface of this cell?

explanation.summary: A macrophage displays 6 different MHC class I molecules and 6 different MHC class II molecules, for 12 in total.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that any given macrophage has on its surface 6 different MHC I molecules from the two alleles at each of the three class I loci (HLA-A, HLA-B, HLA-C), and similarly has 6 different MHC II molecules on its surface. Because macrophages are professional APCs expressing both classes codominantly, the total is 6 plus 6, or 12.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Three would count only one class of loci and only one allele at each, ignoring codominant expression of both haplotypes.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Six is the number for a single class (either class I or class II), not the combined total on a macrophage.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Nine does not correspond to any combination of three loci times two alleles for each class.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Twenty-four double-counts; each class contributes 6 molecules (3 loci times 2 alleles), giving 12 total.

questions.stem: A novel respiratory virus spreads through a community. Some infected people mount effective T cell responses and clear the virus, while others cannot present its peptides effectively and become severely ill. Which feature of MHC genes best explains why at least part of the population is able to fight this new pathogen?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Codominant expression of both parental alleles in each cell

choices.label: B
choices.text: Expression of MHC class I on every nucleated cell

choices.label: C
choices.text: Inheritance of the MHC genes as a haplotype from each parent

choices.label: E
choices.text: Polymorphism, with many different alleles present in the population

explanation.summary: Between-person variation in MHC alleles (polymorphism) ensures that when a new pathogen appears, at least some people can present its peptides.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes MHC genes as the most polymorphic genes in the human genome, with more than 15,000 alleles found in the population. It states that this variation in MHC amino acid sequence confers a survival advantage to the population: if a new pathogen moves through the human population, at least some people will be able to present peptides and fight it effectively, even if others cannot.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Codominance increases the number of different MHC molecules within one person; it does not explain differences in responsiveness between people.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Universal class I expression allows CD8 T cells to survey any nucleated cell, but it does not create the between-person variation described.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Haplotype inheritance describes how the linked genes are passed on, not why different people present different peptides.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Beta-2-microglobulin is not polymorphic and does not form the peptide-binding groove, so it cannot account for population-level differences in presentation.

questions.stem: Two unrelated adults are infected with the original SARS-CoV-2 strain. One remains asymptomatic while the other develops severe disease. Sequencing of their MHC class I genes shows that the asymptomatic person has glutamine at position 144 and arginine at position 151 of one alpha chain, a combination associated with asymptomatic infection. Which mechanism best explains this protective effect?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Altered peptide-binding pockets change which viral peptides are presented

choices.label: B
choices.text: Duplication of the HLA-A locus doubles the number of class I molecules

choices.label: C
choices.text: Enhanced HLA-DM activity accelerates loading of viral peptides onto class I

choices.label: D
choices.text: Increased beta-2-microglobulin expression stabilizes more class I molecules

choices.label: E
choices.text: Loss of the CD8 binding site limits excessive cytotoxic T cell activation

explanation.summary: Amino acid variation in the peptide-binding pockets of MHC class I alters binding affinity for viral peptides and can convey risk or protection.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explains that different people have alpha1 and alpha2 domains that vary by amino acid sequence, conveying different binding affinities for different peptides, so two people infected with the same pathogen may present very different peptides on their MHC I. The clinical correlation on SARS-CoV-2 states that specific variations in amino acids in peptide-binding pockets convey risk or protection, giving glutamine at 144 and arginine at 151 of the alpha chain as an example associated with asymptomatic infection.

whyWrongByChoice.B: The observation is a sequence variation within an existing gene, not a change in gene copy number.
whyWrongByChoice.C: HLA-DM functions in MHC class II loading in endosomes and has no role in loading peptides onto class I.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Beta-2-microglobulin is invariant and does not form the peptide-binding pockets; the finding involves alpha chain sequence variation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The protective variation lies in the peptide-binding pockets, not in the membrane-proximal region where CD8 binds; losing CD8 binding would impair, not improve, cytotoxic responses.

questions.stem: A geneticist maps the MHC region on chromosome 6 and notes that, in addition to the HLA genes, several other genes required for antigen processing are located within this region. Which of the following is encoded within the MHC region?

explanation.summary: The MHC locus on chromosome 6 also contains genes for antigen-processing proteins such as TAP1, TAP2, proteasome components, and HLA-DM.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that other important proteins needed for antigen processing are encoded in the MHC region, and its map of the HLA gene family shows the class II locus containing DM and the proteasome genes TAP1 and TAP2, along with complement proteins (C4, Factor B, C2) and cytokines (TNF, LT) between the class II and class I loci.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Beta-2-microglobulin is specifically noted to be encoded on chromosome 15, outside the MHC loci.
whyWrongByChoice.B: CD8 is a T cell co-receptor and is not listed among the genes of the HLA region.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Perforin is a cytotoxic granule protein released by CD8 T cells; it is not mapped within the MHC region.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Ubiquitin tags proteins for proteasomal degradation but is not among the genes the brick places within the MHC region.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man with melanoma has tumor cells that express a mutated cytosolic protein not found in normal tissue. Tumor-infiltrating CD8+ T cells are shown to kill these tumor cells while sparing adjacent healthy cells. Which of the following best explains how the T cells distinguish tumor cells from healthy cells?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Tumor cells display the intact mutant protein on their surface for TCR binding

choices.label: B
choices.text: Tumor cells express MHC class II, which healthy nonlymphoid cells lack

choices.label: C
choices.text: Tumor cells lose beta-2-microglobulin, which triggers CD8+ T cell attack

choices.label: D
choices.text: Tumor cells present peptides on MHC class I that are not found in healthy cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: Tumor cells release perforin that activates nearby T cells

explanation.summary: MHC class I marks malignant cells for destruction by presenting peptides that are not found in healthy cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that the role of MHC class I is to mark cells infected by intracellular organisms and to mark tumor cells for destruction. Because class I presents peptides from inside the cell, when cells have become malignant, MHC I will present peptides not found in healthy cells. A mutated cytosolic protein is degraded by the proteasome and its peptides displayed on class I, allowing CD8 T cells to recognize and kill the tumor cell.

whyWrongByChoice.A: TCRs are MHC-restricted and recognize only peptide loaded into MHC, not intact protein on a cell surface.
whyWrongByChoice.B: CD8 T cells recognize peptide in MHC class I, not class II; class II expression is not what distinguishes tumor from healthy cells here.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Loss of MHC class I components would reduce CD8 T cell recognition and instead relieve natural killer cell inhibition; it is not how CD8 T cells target tumors.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Perforin is released by activated CD8 T cells to induce apoptosis in targets; tumor cells do not secrete it to activate T cells.

questions.stem: A CD4+ helper T cell clone specific for an influenza peptide is cultured with virus-infected respiratory epithelial cells but does not respond. When dendritic cells that have taken up viral debris are added to the culture, the clone becomes activated. Which of the following best explains the initial lack of response?

choices.label: A
choices.text: CD4 cannot bind MHC molecules on nonhematopoietic cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: Epithelial cells do not express high levels of MHC class II

choices.label: C
choices.text: Epithelial cells lack MHC class I because they are not nucleated

choices.label: D
choices.text: Epithelial cells lack the proteasome needed to generate peptides

choices.label: E
choices.text: Epithelial cells present only 8- to 11-amino-acid peptides on MHC class II

explanation.summary: MHC class II is highly expressed only on professional antigen-presenting cells, so CD4 helper T cells cannot be activated by ordinary infected epithelial cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that MHC class I is expressed on every nucleated cell, but MHC class II is only highly expressed on antigen-presenting cells (macrophages, monocytes, dendritic cells, and B cells) and a subset of cells important in T cell development. Helper T cells use CD4 to bind MHC II, so an infected epithelial cell lacking high levels of class II cannot stimulate the clone, whereas a dendritic cell that has processed viral debris can present the peptide on class II.

whyWrongByChoice.A: CD4 binds MHC class II wherever it is expressed; the problem is that epithelial cells do not display class II at high levels.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Epithelial cells are nucleated and do express MHC class I; the clone is CD4+ and reads class II, so class I is not the issue.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Epithelial cells have proteasomes and can process endogenous viral proteins for class I; the defect is absence of class II presentation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The 8- to 11-amino-acid range applies to MHC class I; class II loads longer peptides, and epithelial cells are not class II-expressing APCs in any case.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman with poorly controlled diabetes develops a skin infection with a fungus that grows extracellularly in the dermis. Fungal proteins are taken up by dermal dendritic cells. Through which pathway are these fungal peptides classically processed and presented?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Direct binding of intact fungal protein by the T cell receptor

choices.label: B
choices.text: MHC class I pathway to CD4+ T cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: MHC class I pathway to CD8+ T cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: MHC class II pathway to CD4+ T cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: MHC class II pathway to CD8+ T cells

explanation.summary: Extracellular pathogens such as most bacteria and fungi are processed through the MHC class II pathway and presented to CD4 helper T cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes two classical ways antigens are processed and presented: intracellular pathogens (like viruses and some bacteria) go through the MHC class I pathway, while extracellular pathogens (like most bacteria and fungi) are processed via the MHC class II pathway. APCs internalize extracellular antigen, digest it into peptides in endosomes, load it onto MHC II, and present it to CD4 helper T cells.

whyWrongByChoice.A: T cell receptors are MHC-restricted and cannot bind intact protein; only B cell receptors recognize whole antigen.
whyWrongByChoice.B: CD4 is the co-receptor for MHC class II, not class I; this pairing does not occur.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The class I pathway classically handles endogenous, cytosolic proteins from intracellular pathogens, not proteins of an extracellular fungus taken up by endocytosis.
whyWrongByChoice.E: CD8 binds MHC class I, not class II; this pairing does not occur.

questions.stem: A monoclonal antibody directed against MHC class I is found to block binding of the CD8 co-receptor without preventing the T cell receptor from contacting the peptide-MHC complex. Which region of the MHC class I molecule does the antibody most likely cover?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The alpha1 domain, forming one wall of the peptide-binding cleft

choices.label: B
choices.text: The alpha2 domain, forming the other wall of the peptide-binding cleft

choices.label: C
choices.text: The bound peptide lying within the groove

choices.label: D
choices.text: The intracytoplasmic tail of the alpha chain

choices.label: E
choices.text: The membrane-proximal base, outside the peptide-binding cleft

explanation.summary: CD8 and CD4 co-receptors bind the base of MHC molecules near the cell membrane, outside the peptide-binding cleft.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explains that CD8 and CD4 are co-receptors that bind the base of MHC molecules and stabilize the interaction of the T cell receptor with the MHC. The figure legend specifies that these co-receptors bind MHC I and II near the cytoplasmic membrane, outside of the peptide-binding cleft. An antibody covering this membrane-proximal region would block CD8 while leaving the TCR's access to the peptide-binding cleft intact.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The alpha1 domain forms part of the peptide-binding cleft that the TCR contacts; blocking it would interfere with TCR recognition, not selectively with CD8.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The alpha2 domain likewise forms the cleft read by the TCR and is not the CD8 contact site.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The peptide is recognized by the TCR; covering it would prevent TCR binding, which the stem says is preserved.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The intracytoplasmic region is inside the cell and inaccessible to an extracellular antibody; CD8 binds the extracellular base.

questions.stem: In an experimental antigen-presenting cell line, MHC class II molecules are synthesized normally but accumulate in the endoplasmic reticulum and fail to reach endosomal compartments. Which of the following chaperone functions is most likely lost in these cells?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Beta-2-microglobulin-mediated stabilization of the alpha chain

choices.label: B
choices.text: HLA-DM-catalyzed exchange of CLIP for antigenic peptide

choices.label: C
choices.text: Invariant chain-directed trafficking of MHC class II toward endosomes

choices.label: D
choices.text: TAP-mediated transport of peptides from the cytosol into the ER

choices.label: E
choices.text: Tapasin-mediated tethering of MHC molecules near TAP

explanation.summary: Beyond blocking the groove, the invariant chain promotes movement of MHC class II from the ER to the Golgi and then into the endocytic pathway.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that the invariant chain promotes MHC II expression in multiple ways: first, it stabilizes MHC II prior to peptide binding and its CLIP segment blocks the groove; second, it promotes the movement of the MHC II complex from the ER to the Golgi, then to the endocytic pathway. Class II that is made normally but never leaves the ER for endosomes points to loss of this trafficking function.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Beta-2-microglobulin is a subunit of MHC class I, not a chaperone for class II.
whyWrongByChoice.B: HLA-DM acts later, within the acidic endosome, to swap CLIP for peptide; its loss would leave class II at the surface bearing CLIP, not stuck in the ER.
whyWrongByChoice.D: TAP transports peptides for MHC class I loading and has no role in moving class II out of the ER.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Tapasin is a class I chaperone that brings MHC I close to TAP; it does not traffic class II.

questions.stem: A dendritic cell culture is treated with a drug that prevents acidification of endosomes and phagosomes. Uptake of extracellular antigen and synthesis of MHC class II are unaffected. Which step of MHC class II peptide loading is most directly impaired?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Association of beta-2-microglobulin with the class I alpha chain

choices.label: B
choices.text: Binding of the invariant chain to newly made MHC class II in the ER

choices.label: C
choices.text: Degradation of the invariant chain, leaving only CLIP in the groove

choices.label: D
choices.text: Stabilization of the TCR-MHC class II interaction by CD4 at the surface

choices.label: E
choices.text: Transport of cytosolic peptides into the ER by the TAP transporter

explanation.summary: The acidic environment of endosomes and phagosomes dissolves the invariant chain except for CLIP, a prerequisite for HLA-DM to exchange CLIP for antigenic peptide.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explains that after the invariant chain moves MHC II from the ER through the Golgi into the endocytic pathway, the acidic environment of phagosomes and endosomes dissolves the invariant chain except for the CLIP fragment bound in the groove. Only then can HLA-DM catalyze exchange of CLIP for an antigenic peptide. Preventing acidification blocks this invariant chain degradation step.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Beta-2-microglobulin is part of MHC class I and assembles in the ER, not in acidic endosomes.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The invariant chain binds MHC II in the ER, a neutral compartment unaffected by loss of endosomal acidification.
whyWrongByChoice.D: CD4 stabilization occurs at the cell surface during T cell recognition, after loading is complete.
whyWrongByChoice.E: TAP transport into the ER belongs to the MHC class I pathway and does not depend on endosomal pH.

questions.stem: A B cell whose antigen receptor binds tetanus toxoid internalizes the toxoid and later displays toxoid-derived peptides on MHC class II to a CD4+ helper T cell. By which mechanism did the B cell take up the antigen?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Leakage from a phagosome into the cytosol

choices.label: D
choices.text: Transport of the toxoid through TAP

explanation.summary: B cells are not phagocytes; they internalize antigen by antigen-receptor-mediated endocytosis and then process it for MHC class II presentation.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that phagocytes such as monocytes, macrophages, and dendritic cells take up exogenous antigen by phagocytosis, but that B cells, while not phagocytes, are capable of antigen-receptor-mediated endocytosis and subsequent processing of antigen. Either phagocytosis or endocytosis allows generation of cleaved peptides for loading onto MHC II.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Leakage from a phagosome into the cytosol describes cross-presentation onto MHC class I, not the uptake step in a B cell presenting on class II.
whyWrongByChoice.C: B cells are specifically described as not being phagocytes; phagocytosis is the route used by macrophages, monocytes, and dendritic cells.
whyWrongByChoice.D: TAP transports cytosolic peptides into the ER for MHC class I loading; it does not bring extracellular antigen into the cell.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Ubiquitination marks cytosolic proteins for proteasomal degradation and is not a mechanism of antigen uptake.

questions.stem: In a virus-infected hepatocyte, newly synthesized viral proteins are covalently tagged with a small protein that directs them to a cytosolic complex where they are digested into peptide fragments. Which of the following is the tag?

explanation.summary: Ubiquitin labels endogenous proteins so that they are trafficked to the proteasome for digestion.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explains that endogenous proteins are constantly recycled by the proteasome: proteins are labeled by ubiquitin, and ubiquitinated proteins are trafficked to the proteasome for digestion and reuse of amino acids. The resulting peptide fragments are then transported by TAP into the ER for MHC class I loading.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Beta-2-microglobulin is a structural subunit of MHC class I, not a tag on cytosolic proteins.
whyWrongByChoice.B: CLIP is the fragment of the invariant chain that occupies the MHC class II groove; it is not a degradation tag.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The invariant chain is a chaperone for MHC class II in the ER and endocytic pathway; it does not target proteins for degradation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Tapasin is an ER chaperone that brings MHC class I close to TAP; it does not mark proteins for the proteasome.

questions.stem: A mutant cell line has functional TAP, and proteasome-derived peptides are readily detected inside the endoplasmic reticulum. Nevertheless, MHC class I molecules are loaded inefficiently and surface expression of class I is low. Loss of which protein best explains this defect?

explanation.summary: Tapasin brings MHC class I close to TAP so that transported peptides can be loaded into the class I groove.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes tapasin as a chaperone protein that brings MHC I close to TAP so the peptide can be loaded from TAP into MHC I. When peptides reach the ER normally (intact TAP) but class I still fails to load, the missing link is the tethering chaperone. Without efficient loading, MHC I remains unstable and surface expression falls.

whyWrongByChoice.A: CD8 is a T cell co-receptor that binds class I on the cell surface; it plays no role in loading peptide inside the ER.
whyWrongByChoice.B: HLA-DM catalyzes CLIP exchange for MHC class II in endosomes; it has no role in class I loading in the ER.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The invariant chain is a class II chaperone; its absence would not impair loading of class I.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Ubiquitin acts upstream, tagging proteins for the proteasome; the stem shows peptides are already generated and present in the ER.

questions.stem: A cell line lacking TAP synthesizes normal amounts of MHC class I alpha chain and beta-2-microglobulin, yet flow cytometry shows very little MHC class I on the cell surface. Which of the following best explains the low surface expression?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Beta-2-microglobulin cannot associate with the alpha chain without TAP

choices.label: B
choices.text: CD8+ T cells rapidly kill cells that display empty MHC class I

choices.label: C
choices.text: HLA-DM strips empty MHC class I from the cell surface

choices.label: D
choices.text: MHC class I that is not loaded with peptide is unstable and is degraded

choices.label: E
choices.text: Unloaded MHC class I is retained in the ER by the invariant chain

explanation.summary: Peptide loading stabilizes MHC class I; unloaded class I is unstable and is eventually degraded, so it is not expressed on the surface.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that if a peptide can be presented by MHC I, the MHC I/peptide complex will stabilize and be transported to the cell surface, but if MHC I is not loaded with peptide, it is unstable and eventually will be degraded. The case connection reinforces this: MHC is not expressed if peptides are not loaded. Without TAP, no peptides enter the ER, so class I never stabilizes and surface levels fall.

whyWrongByChoice.A: TAP transports peptides; it is not required for the alpha chain and beta-2-microglobulin to associate.
whyWrongByChoice.B: CD8 T cells recognize peptide loaded in class I; empty class I does not trigger them, and the stem describes a cell line, not killing.
whyWrongByChoice.C: HLA-DM works in the class II endosomal pathway; it does not act on class I at the cell surface.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The invariant chain binds MHC class II, not class I, and is not the reason empty class I fails to reach the surface.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old woman is diagnosed with an autoimmune disease that is strongly associated with a particular HLA allele. Which of the following best explains how an MHC allele increases the risk of autoimmune disease?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The allele binds certain self-peptides well and activates cognate T cells

choices.label: B
choices.text: The allele cannot be loaded with peptide and is rapidly degraded

choices.label: C
choices.text: The allele fails to inhibit natural killer cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: The allele is expressed on erythrocytes, exposing them to CD8+ T cells

choices.label: E
choices.text: The allele is inherited dominantly rather than codominantly

explanation.summary: MHC alleles differ in their ability to present self-peptides; risk alleles are very good at binding certain self-peptides and activating cognate T cells.
explanation.whyCorrect: The clinical correlation explains that, just as different alleles of MHC differ in their ability to present peptides from pathogens, they also differ in their ability to present self-peptides. Some MHC alleles are associated with risk of autoimmune disease, likely because those alleles are very good at binding certain self-peptides and activating cognate T cells.

whyWrongByChoice.B: An allele that could not be loaded would be unstable and degraded, reducing presentation rather than driving self-reactive T cell activation.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Natural killer cell inhibition by class I relates to detecting cells that have lost MHC, not to presenting self-peptides to T cells.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Erythrocytes lack a nucleus and do not express MHC class I; MHC allele-associated autoimmunity is not about red cell expression.
whyWrongByChoice.E: All MHC genes are expressed codominantly; the mode of inheritance does not differ between risk and non-risk alleles.

questions.stem: A 2-month-old girl has been hospitalized repeatedly since birth for severe, recurrent respiratory, eye, and skin infections caused by fungal, viral, and bacterial organisms. Laboratory studies show markedly reduced numbers of both T and B lymphocytes and low serum immunoglobulin levels. Genetic testing points to a defect in the enzyme that introduces double-strand breaks so that antigen-receptor gene segments can be cut and rejoined. Which of the following enzymes is most likely deficient in this patient?

choices.label: B
choices.text: Neonatal Fc receptor for immunoglobulin G (FcRn)

explanation.summary: RAG-1 and RAG-2 cut DNA to permit V(D)J recombination; their loss prevents BCR and TCR generation, causing SCID.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that RAG (recombination-activating gene 1 and 2) is the enzyme responsible for introducing breaks in DNA so that V, D, and J gene segments can be joined. Without RAG, V(D)J recombination cannot occur and neither BCRs nor TCRs can be generated, producing a severe deficiency of both B and T cells. This matches the case connection of an infant with combined immunodeficiency (SCID) treated with hematopoietic stem cell transplantation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: A complement pathway defect would impair innate opsonization/lysis but would not deplete T and B cells or block antigen-receptor assembly.
whyWrongByChoice.B: FcRn mediates placental transfer of IgG and prolongs its half-life; it does not affect V(D)J recombination or lymphocyte development.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The poly-Ig receptor transcytoses IgA across mucosal epithelium and has no role in generating lymphocytes or their receptors.
whyWrongByChoice.E: TdT adds random nucleotides at segment junctions to create junctional diversity; its loss reduces diversity but does not abolish receptor generation or wipe out both lineages.

questions.stem: A researcher sequencing rearranged antigen-receptor loci finds a B-cell receptor chain and a T-cell receptor chain that were each assembled using only V and J gene segments, with no D segment involved. These two chains most likely correspond to which of the following variable domains?

explanation.summary: The BCR light chain and the TCR alpha chain build their variable domains from V and J segments only.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explains that the BCR light chain (V(L)) and the TCR alpha chain (V(alpha)) are generated using only V and J segments, which is why the 'D' in V(D)J is placed in parentheses. The BCR heavy chain (V(H)) and TCR beta chain (V(beta)) additionally use a D segment.

whyWrongByChoice.A: V(beta) uses a D segment; only V(alpha) among the two is limited to V and J.
whyWrongByChoice.B: V(H) uses a D segment, so this pair is not restricted to V and J.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Both V(H) (heavy chain) and V(beta) additionally use a D segment, so neither is built from V and J alone.
whyWrongByChoice.D: V(H) uses V, D, and J segments; only V(L) is limited to V and J.

questions.stem: During assembly of a developing B cell's antigen receptor, extra nucleotides are inserted at the boundaries where the V, D, and J segments are being joined, generating sequences not encoded in the germline. Which of the following processes and mediators best accounts for this added diversity?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Isotype switching of the heavy-chain constant region

choices.label: B
choices.text: Nucleotide addition at junctions by TdT

choices.label: C
choices.text: Random pairing of heavy and light chains

choices.label: D
choices.text: Selection of B cells by clonal selection

explanation.summary: Junctional diversity comes from terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase (TdT) adding random nucleotides at the V(D)J junctions.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes junctional diversity as the random addition of nucleotides at segment junctions before they are joined, catalyzed by terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase (TdT). This is why CDR3, which spans the junctions, is the most diverse and is not germline-encoded.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Isotype switching changes the constant region class and does not add nucleotides to the variable region junctions.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Random heavy/light chain pairing is combinatorial diversity, which reshuffles whole domains rather than inserting nucleotides at junctions.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Clonal selection expands antigen-specific B cells; it does not create receptor sequence diversity.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Somatic hypermutation introduces point mutations after antigen encounter, not junctional insertions during development.

questions.stem: An immunologist is comparing secreted antibody isotypes and wants to identify the class that provides the greatest number of antigen-binding sites per secreted molecule, giving it especially high avidity early in an immune response. Which isotype fits this description?

explanation.summary: Secreted IgM is a pentamer with 10 antigen-binding sites, giving it the highest avidity of the isotypes.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick teaches that secreted IgM exists as a pentamer joined by a J chain; with two binding sites per monomer, the pentamer has ten antigen-binding sites. This gives IgM the highest avidity (the combination of individual affinities) and makes it effective early, when it is the first class produced.

whyWrongByChoice.A: IgA is a dimer at mucosal surfaces (and a monomer in blood), giving at most four binding sites, fewer than pentameric IgM.
whyWrongByChoice.B: IgD is a monomer with only two binding sites and is secreted at very low levels.
whyWrongByChoice.C: IgE is a monomer with two binding sites and is mostly bound to its receptor on mast cells.
whyWrongByChoice.D: IgG is a monomer with two binding sites; although the most abundant serum antibody, it does not have the most binding sites per molecule.

questions.stem: Two weeks after a first exposure to a vaccine antigen, a patient's germinal-center B cells accumulate point mutations in the genes encoding their variable domains, and B cells whose receptors bind the antigen more tightly are preferentially selected to survive. Which of the following statements best characterizes this process?

choices.label: A
choices.text: It occurs after antigen recognition and increases BCR affinity for antigen

choices.label: B
choices.text: It occurs after antigen recognition and increases diversity of TCR specificity

choices.label: C
choices.text: It occurs before antigen recognition and increases BCR affinity for antigen

choices.label: D
choices.text: It occurs in both B and T cells to change the constant region class

choices.label: E
choices.text: It occurs prior to antigen recognition and increases diversity of TCR specificity

explanation.summary: Somatic hypermutation occurs in B cells after antigen recognition and raises BCR affinity through affinity maturation.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that somatic hypermutation occurs in activated B cells after antigen recognition, introducing random mutations primarily in the CDRs (hypervariable regions) of the V(H) domains. B cells whose mutated receptors bind antigen best are selected to survive and proliferate, so the affinity of the repertoire rises. This distinguishes it from V(D)J recombination, which occurs before antigen recognition in both B and T cells.

whyWrongByChoice.B: T cells do not undergo somatic hypermutation; once mature, the TCR does not change.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Somatic hypermutation happens after, not before, antigen recognition; V(D)J recombination is the developmental process that precedes antigen exposure.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Changing the constant-region class describes isotype switching, not somatic hypermutation, and hypermutation is a B-cell-only event.
whyWrongByChoice.E: It affects B cells, not TCRs, and follows rather than precedes antigen recognition; TCRs do not undergo somatic hypermutation.

questions.stem: A full-term newborn is found to have protective serum levels of antibody against tetanus toxin, matching the mother's immunity, even though the infant has never been vaccinated. These maternally derived antibodies were transported across the placenta by a specific Fc receptor. Which antibody isotype is responsible for this protection?

explanation.summary: IgG is the only isotype that crosses the placenta, carried by the neonatal Fc receptor (FcRn).
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that IgG is the most abundant serum antibody and the only class able to cross the placenta. The secreted neonatal Fc receptor (FcRn) mediates placental transfer of IgG and also prolongs its half-life in the circulation, explaining protective maternal IgG in the newborn.

whyWrongByChoice.A: IgA is concentrated at mucosal surfaces and passes to infants mainly via breast milk, not across the placenta.
whyWrongByChoice.B: IgD is secreted only at very low levels and functions in naive B cell signaling, not in placental transfer.
whyWrongByChoice.C: IgE is mostly bound to mast cells and mediates allergy/anti-parasite responses; it does not cross the placenta.
whyWrongByChoice.E: IgM is a large pentamer that does not cross the placenta.

questions.stem: A researcher studying breast milk and saliva isolates the predominant antibody at these mucosal surfaces. It exists there as a dimer joined by a J chain and reaches the secretions by being transcytosed across epithelial cells by a dedicated receptor. Which isotype and transport receptor pair is described?

choices.label: A
choices.text: IgA transported by the polymeric immunoglobulin receptor (pIgR)

choices.label: B
choices.text: IgE transported by the high-affinity receptor FcERI

choices.label: D
choices.text: IgG transported by the neonatal Fc receptor (FcRn)

choices.label: E
choices.text: IgM transported by the polymeric immunoglobulin receptor (pIgR)

explanation.summary: Mucosal IgA is a J-chain-joined dimer that crosses epithelium via the polymeric immunoglobulin receptor (pIgR).
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick teaches that IgA is the most abundant antibody at mucosal surfaces (tears, saliva, breast milk), where it exists as a dimer joined by a J chain. It enters the mucosa through transcytosis across epithelial cells mediated by the polymeric immunoglobulin receptor (pIgR); in blood it circulates as a monomer.

whyWrongByChoice.B: FcERI binds IgE on mast cells and basophils for allergic/anti-parasite responses; it is not a mucosal transcytosis receptor.
whyWrongByChoice.C: FcgammaRIIIa (CD16) on NK cells mediates ADCC by IgG; it does not transport antibody into secretions.
whyWrongByChoice.D: FcRn transports IgG across the placenta and prolongs IgG half-life; it does not deliver the dimeric mucosal antibody.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Although IgM also uses a J chain, the dominant mucosal secretory antibody delivered by pIgR is dimeric IgA, not IgM.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old man with seasonal hay fever develops sneezing, itchy watery eyes, and nasal congestion each spring. His symptoms result from an antibody that is bound to Fc receptors on mast cells; when pollen cross-links these antibodies, the mast cells aggregate the receptors and degranulate, releasing inflammatory mediators. Which antibody isotype and receptor mediate this reaction?

choices.label: A
choices.text: IgA bound to FcalphaR on phagocytes

choices.label: B
choices.text: IgD bound to receptors on naive B cells

choices.label: C
choices.text: IgE bound to FcERI on mast cells

choices.label: D
choices.text: IgG bound to FcgammaR on phagocytes

explanation.summary: IgE bound to FcERI on mast cells and basophils triggers degranulation in allergic reactions.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick explains that IgE's function is mediated by binding of its Fc region to the high-affinity IgE receptor (FcERI) on mast cells, eosinophils, and basophils. In classic allergic reactions, allergen cross-links receptor-bound IgE, causing receptor aggregation, mast cell activation, and degranulation with release of inflammatory mediators, producing edema, itching, and congestion.

whyWrongByChoice.A: IgA and its low-affinity FcalphaR act in mucosal immunity, not in mast-cell-driven hypersensitivity.
whyWrongByChoice.B: IgD functions in naive B cell signaling and has no role in mast cell degranulation.
whyWrongByChoice.D: IgG on phagocyte FcgammaR mediates opsonization and ADCC, not immediate mast cell degranulation of allergy.
whyWrongByChoice.E: IgM activates the classical complement pathway; it is not the antibody pre-armed on mast cells for allergy.

questions.stem: An investigator enzymatically separates an IgG molecule into its Y-shaped fragments. She wants the fragment that binds complement proteins and Fc receptors to carry out the antibody's effector functions, rather than the fragment that contacts antigen. Which portion of the antibody should she isolate?

choices.label: E
choices.text: The variable domain of the light chain

explanation.summary: The Fc region is the stem of the Y and carries out effector functions by binding complement and Fc receptors.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes the antibody as roughly Y-shaped: the two arms are the antigen-binding fragments (Fab) involved in antigen recognition, while the stem or base is the crystallizable fragment (Fc) responsible for effector functions, specifically binding complement and Fc receptors.

whyWrongByChoice.A: CDR3 is a hypervariable antigen-contacting loop, part of antigen recognition, not effector function.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The Fab region is the antigen-binding arm, not the part that engages complement and Fc receptors.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The hinge is a flexible connector between the arms; it provides mobility, not effector binding.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The light-chain variable domain helps form the antigen-binding site, so it is part of antigen recognition rather than effector function.

questions.stem: A mature B cell circulating between the blood and secondary lymphoid organs has not yet encountered its cognate antigen. Flow cytometry is used to characterize the immunoglobulin isotypes displayed on its surface. Which of the following is most likely observed?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Pentameric IgM secreted into the plasma

choices.label: B
choices.text: Secreted IgA as a mucosal dimer

explanation.summary: Naive B cells co-express surface IgM and IgD before encountering antigen.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that naive B cells are mature B cells that have not encountered their cognate antigen and that they express the mu and delta heavy-chain constant domains, so they carry both IgM and IgD on their surface (with the same variable and light-chain regions). Secretion of antibody and any class switching occur only after activation.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Secreted pentameric IgM is released only after the B cell is activated; a naive B cell displays membrane IgM (and IgD) rather than secreting pentamer.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Secreted dimeric IgA is a product of activated, class-switched plasma cells at mucosal surfaces, not a naive B cell's surface receptor.
whyWrongByChoice.C: IgE bound to FcERI is displayed on mast cells and basophils, not on the surface of a naive B cell.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Surface IgG appears only after activation and isotype switching, not on a naive, antigen-inexperienced B cell.

questions.stem: While mapping which parts of a B-cell receptor's variable domain contact antigen, a researcher identifies three loops called the complementarity-determining regions. One of them is far more variable than the others because it spans the junctions created during recombination and is not encoded in the germline. Which region is being described?

choices.label: D
choices.text: The constant domain of the heavy chain

explanation.summary: CDR3 is the most diverse complementarity-determining region because it is formed at the recombination junctions and is not germline-encoded.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes three regions of the V(H) and V(L) domains that contact antigen, called CDR1, CDR2, and CDR3. CDR1 and CDR2 are encoded by the V gene segments, whereas CDR3 is encoded by the junctional regions. Because its diversity comes from combinatorial and junctional (non-germline) mechanisms, CDR3 is the most diverse of the three.

whyWrongByChoice.A: CDR1 is encoded within the germline V segment and is far less variable than CDR3.
whyWrongByChoice.B: CDR2, like CDR1, is encoded by the V gene segment and is not the most diverse loop.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The heavy-chain constant domain determines isotype and effector function; it does not contact antigen and is not hypervariable.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The hinge provides flexibility between the arms and is not one of the antigen-contacting CDRs.

questions.stem: After receiving help from CD4+ helper T cells in a germinal center, an activated B cell that originally made IgM begins secreting IgG that binds the same epitope with identical specificity. Which of the following best describes the change that has occurred?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Clonal selection converted the T cell into an antibody-secreting cell

choices.label: B
choices.text: Combinatorial diversity paired a new heavy chain with a new light chain

choices.label: C
choices.text: Isotype switching changed the heavy-chain constant region

choices.label: D
choices.text: Somatic hypermutation replaced the constant region of the antibody

choices.label: E
choices.text: V(D)J recombination rebuilt the variable domain to recognize a new antigen

explanation.summary: Isotype switching swaps the heavy-chain constant region (e.g., IgM to IgG) with CD4+ T cell help, keeping antigen specificity unchanged.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick teaches that activated B cells receiving help from CD4+ helper T cells can undergo isotype (class) switching, changing from expressing IgM and IgD to IgG, IgA, or IgE. Only the heavy-chain constant domain changes, so the antigen specificity determined by the variable domains is preserved; most B cells switch to become IgG-producing cells.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Clonal selection expands antigen-specific B cells; helper T cells provide signals but do not themselves become antibody-secreting cells.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Combinatorial diversity from heavy/light chain pairing occurs during development and would change the antigen recognized, not just the isotype.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Somatic hypermutation mutates the variable-domain CDRs to fine-tune affinity; it does not replace the constant region or switch class.
whyWrongByChoice.E: V(D)J recombination builds the variable domain during development and would alter, not preserve, antigen specificity; it is not how a mature B cell changes class.

questions.stem: A researcher isolates an antibody-secreting plasma cell from the bone marrow of a patient with a chronic parasitic infection and sequences the gene encoding the heavy-chain constant domains of the antibody it produces. The expressed constant-region gene is C-epsilon. Which antibody class is this plasma cell producing?

explanation.summary: The Greek letter of the heavy-chain constant domain names the isotype: C-epsilon encodes IgE.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick teaches that there are five possible heavy-chain constant domains (gamma, alpha, mu, epsilon, and delta) and that the heavy chain determines an antibody's class or isotype. The Greek letters correspond to the English isotype names: C-gamma encodes IgG, C-alpha encodes IgA, C-mu encodes IgM, C-epsilon encodes IgE, and C-delta encodes IgD. A plasma cell expressing C-epsilon is therefore secreting IgE, the class involved in helminth defense.

whyWrongByChoice.A: IgA is encoded by the C-alpha constant-region gene, not C-epsilon.
whyWrongByChoice.B: IgD is encoded by the C-delta constant-region gene.
whyWrongByChoice.D: IgG is encoded by the C-gamma constant-region gene.
whyWrongByChoice.E: IgM is encoded by the C-mu constant-region gene.

questions.stem: A laboratory characterizes the light chains of an immunoglobulin purified from a healthy donor's serum. Each light chain consists of one variable domain and one constant domain. The constant domain of an immunoglobulin light chain can be which of the following?

explanation.summary: There are two possible light-chain constant domains, kappa and lambda, encoded by different genes.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick states that each BCR or Ig light chain is made up of a variable domain (V-L) and a constant domain (C-L), and that there are two possible light-chain constant domains, kappa and lambda, which are encoded by different genes. The five constant domains gamma, alpha, mu, epsilon, and delta belong to heavy chains, not light chains, and determine isotype.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Alpha and delta are heavy-chain constant domains (IgA and IgD).
whyWrongByChoice.B: Kappa is a light-chain constant domain, but epsilon is the heavy-chain constant domain of IgE.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Gamma and mu are heavy-chain constant domains (IgG and IgM), not light-chain constant domains.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Lambda is a light-chain constant domain, but mu is the heavy-chain constant domain of IgM.

questions.stem: A biochemist treats purified IgG with a reagent that selectively reduces disulfide bonds and observes that the two heavy chains separate from one another. Prior to treatment, the two heavy chains were held together by which of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A joining (J) chain between the Fc regions

choices.label: B
choices.text: A single disulfide bond between the VH domains

choices.label: C
choices.text: A single disulfide bond in the CH1 domain

choices.label: D
choices.text: Two disulfide bonds at the hinge region

choices.label: E
choices.text: Two disulfide bonds within the light chains

explanation.summary: The two heavy chains of a BCR/Ig are connected by two disulfide bonds at the flexible hinge region.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick describes BCRs as glycoproteins made of two large heavy chains and two smaller light chains. The two heavy chains are connected by two disulfide bonds at the hinge region, a flexible region that allows the molecule to twist and bend. Each heavy chain connects to a single light chain by a single disulfide bond.

whyWrongByChoice.A: The J chain joins separate antibody monomers into pentameric IgM or dimeric IgA; it does not hold the two heavy chains of one monomer together.
whyWrongByChoice.B: The variable domains form the antigen-binding site and are not where the heavy chains are covalently linked to each other.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The single disulfide bond in the Fab arm links a heavy chain to its light chain; it does not join the two heavy chains to each other.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Light chains attach to heavy chains by a single disulfide bond each; they are not the link between the two heavy chains.

questions.stem: Two unrelated healthy adults are found to have slightly different amino acid sequences in the constant domains of their IgG heavy chains, although both produce fully functional IgG. Which of the following terms refers to each person's own set of constant-domain genes?

explanation.summary: Small person-to-person differences in constant-domain genes define an individual's allotype.
explanation.whyCorrect: The brick notes that there are very few differences between the genes (and proteins) for the constant domains between people, but these differences are acknowledged by referring to each person's set of constant-domain genes as their allotype. This is distinct from isotype, which is the class determined by which heavy-chain constant domain is used.

whyWrongByChoice.B: A clone is a group of B cells that share the same idiotype; it does not describe inherited constant-domain differences.
whyWrongByChoice.C: An epitope is the portion of an antigen that an antigen receptor binds; it is not a property of the antibody's constant region.
whyWrongByChoice.D: The idiotype is the unique antigen-binding surface generated by the CDRs of the variable domains, not a person's constant-domain gene set.
